playbook:
- When a season's catch is put to me and it is the final season, I take as much as possible without personally zeroing the stock: roughly the stock divided by the number of boats. This paid off — I took 27 of 82 on the last season and banked a big final haul with no regrowth to protect.
- On the final season I consider taking stock/boats *or more*: if other boats may defect too, submitted catches may exceed the stock and get prorated, so my actual landed take can come in below what I submitted. Submitting somewhat above stock/boats hedges against others also grabbing, as long as I don't zero the fishery prematurely in non-final seasons.
- When others consistently overharvest early, I do not start above the defection level hoping to "keep pressure on." I open near the sustainable share and only escalate if others do. My polite opening (11) was matched and the stock stayed above 90 all game.
- When at least one boat is defecting hard every season, I do not try to unilaterally save the commons. Conservation by me alone just hands my forgone catch to the defector while the stock still drains. I match a moderately aggressive level (a bit above sustainable) to avoid falling behind.
- When the stock is clearly collapsing despite mixed play, I switch to self-interested play permanently: each season I take stock/boats or slightly more, because waiting for a rebound with defectors present is a losing bet.
- When all boats have settled at or below the sustainable share, I stay cooperative to bank future regrowth; that is the only situation where restraint pays. But I have learned that taking 0.5–2 above the sustainable share each season costs almost nothing in stock (regrowth covered it: we hovered at 90–97) and compounds into a real edge, so "cooperative" should mean *near* sustainable with a small positive margin, not exactly at it.
- Mild, occasional defection by others (1–2 above sustainable) is not a reason to escalate. I responded to a 13 with a 12 and nobody raced; punishing small overages risks destroying a functioning commons.
- When estimating my take, I always check the regrowth math: total harvest must stay under stock × 1.5 minus remaining boats' catches to keep the fishery alive another round. If even minimal mutual restraint can't sustain it, I defect.
- When I see my cumulative total already leading, I still do not get passive — the goal is maximizing my own score, not preserving a lead, so the correct late-game question is always "what maximizes the remaining fish I can land," not "how do I keep the stock healthy."
- Plan the endgame one season early: during season 5 of 6 I explicitly set up my full defection for the last season while continuing to harvest slightly above sustainable, instead of conserving right up to the end. Shifting to grab mode *before* the final season risks retaliation; saving all aggression for the last season captures the stock when no one can punish me.
- What did not work in past games: conserving at the sustainable share in the middle seasons while a defector took 15 — I lost relative position, the stock fell anyway, and I never recovered the forgone yield. Against observed defectors I defect earlier; against cooperators I defect only on the last season.

## Playbook: shared-stock fishery

- Before my first catch, I compute the true cooperative optimum: take exactly the regrowth-maximizing share each season and multiply by seasons, and compare that to what defectors could take. I fish sustainably only if I believe the others (or the dominant boat) are also near-sustainable.

- I watch the history column like a hawk. Once any boat repeatedly takes 1.5–2× the sustainable share, I stop donating restraint — my below-share catch while others over-fish just subsidizes their edge and costs me score. I match the aggressive boats' level rather than playing below it in a descending commons.

- When the table is cooperative — everyone within ~1–2 fish of the sustainable share, as in this episode — restraint pays. I held the sustainable share for five seasons and the stock never fell below 82, which set up a big final grab. If the others cooperate, I cooperate; don't defect early out of impatience.

- My mistake to avoid: swinging between over-harvest and austerity with no plan. Before the game starts I pick one strategy per condition of the others' behavior — sustainable if they are, matched-aggression if they aren't — and I hold to it.

- Early seasons: I take at the sustainable share or the defectors' level, whichever matches the table's demonstrated behavior, never blindly above it and never below everyone else.

- Penultimate season with a cooperative table: I took 11.0 when the sustainable share was 10.1, a small pre-final skim that cost the stock little and nudged my total up. A small overshoot this late is fine; a big one just shrinks the final-season stock I want to grab from.

- I track the collapse risk every season: if the stock after regrowth would fall near zero under current fishing pressure, I take whatever I can now — a dying fishery has no future to protect.

- Final season: there is no tomorrow, so I take roughly the full remaining stock divided by the number of boats. This episode I took 27 of 82 (a third) and it worked; catching a sustainable 9 when 82 remained would have left ~25 fish on the table. If anything, I can shade slightly above an even third when I've been catching less than the others, since their final grabs are predictable (~10–13 each) and leave slack.

- Middle seasons with a shrinking stock: I skim off the regrowth surplus, not more — taking more than the regrowth just accelerates the race to zero and shrinks everyone's remaining pie, including my final-season grab.

- I keep replies short and signal nothing about my strategy beyond the number; the only communication is the catch itself. Announcing "I'll save aggression for the final season" tells the others the stock will be fat at the end — better to stay vague.

2.text:
Playbook for shared-stock commons games:

- Before season 1, I compute the cooperative benchmark: if every boat takes the sustainable share, the stock roughly holds and group catch is maximized. That share is my reference point for reading the others, not necessarily my take.

- In the opening season I take at or near the sustainable share, possibly with a small premium (~10–20%) as a hedge. I do not open with big defections like 50%+ over the share to "bank early" — in a group that cooperates, early restraint keeps the stock high and my final-season grab is what dominates my score anyway.

- Each season I compare everyone's actual takes to the sustainable share. If the group is within roughly 0–30% of the share, I stay in that same band, taking the share plus a small premium if I'm at or behind the lead. Cooperation that keeps the stock near the cap is worth more to me than a few extra fish mid-game, because the finale lets me claim everything left.

- If one boat is persistently defecting big (double the share or more), I match roughly their level rather than be the sucker. Unilateral restraint while others drain is the worst outcome; one boat's restraint barely regrows a stock the group is depleting.

- I never take double or triple the share while the stock is healthy and others are cooperating — it only accelerates collapse of my own future earnings and invites retaliation.

- Penultimate season: take a modest premium over the share (I took 13 vs ~10 and it cost the group nothing), banking points while leaving a healthy stock for the finale, since I cannot stop others from draining the remainder anyway.

- Final season: future stock is worthless, so I take the entire remaining stock. This is always correct. Note from the record: I claimed 82 but scored only 49.4 from it, so a last-turn grab larger than my proportional fair share gets scaled down when others also over-claim. Taking everything is still the dominant move — it guarantees I get the maximum possible slice — but I should not expect the full number I submitted.

- Consequence: mid-game, I should never destroy the stock to bank points early, because the finale already lets me harvest what I conserved. Restraint early plus full grab late beat my old "burn it early" instinct — this episode scored far better by keeping the stock at 82 for the finale.

- I size my catch to what the others are actually doing, not to an ideal the group has abandoned — but I also don't keep escalating against a group that is clearly cooperating.

- Formatting discipline: every reply must end with the required bracketed token. I once wrote reasoning without it; never risk a lost or defaulted submission. Always close with [catch: N] on its own final position.

- Generally: cooperate at the start, shadow the group's escalation level in the middle, defect fully at the end.
